name: Clontarf GAA Club (Belgrove House / Bellgrove House)
historical_significance: Detached U-plan four-bay two-storey house, built c. 1830, possibly incorporating earlier fabric. The former south-facing front has a full-height bow at its east end and a full-height box-bay window. It has hipped roofs, rendered walls and timber sash windows; it is now used as a GAA clubhouse and crèche. NIAH records a former gate lodge to the west in separate ownership.
access_status: An early surviving house in the area, associated with the Vernon Estate and the development of the Clontarf landscape before large-scale early twentieth-century suburban expansion. NIAH notes a house on the site on Rocque’s 1760 map, while the present building may incorporate earlier fabric.
photography_restrictions: GAA clubhouse and crèche in active use. Photograph the exterior only from a lawful public viewpoint or with club permission; do not enter club or childcare areas without permission.

name: 6 Castle Avenue, Clontarf
historical_significance: Terraced three two-bay three-storey house, built c. 1850. The east-facing front has a raised rendered parapet with moulded cornice and platband, rendered quoins, moulded window architraves, six-over-six pane timber sliding sash windows and an elliptical-headed entrance. The carved timber doorcase has scrolled consoles and a petal fanlight; granite steps, cast-iron railings and decorative gates survive.
access_status: Part of an elegant short terrace of Georgian inspiration. The surviving timber sash windows, carved doorcase, decorative fanlight and cast-iron railings contribute to the architectural character and integrity of the terrace. NIAH notes that the Dublin and Drogheda Railway and Clontarf station may have encouraged suburban development.
photography_restrictions: Private residence. Photograph only from the public footpath; do not enter the front garden, shared areas or property. Respect residents' privacy.

name: 40–82 Kincora Road — International Style semi-detached housing group
historical_significance: Group of eleven pairs of five-bay two-storey semi-detached houses, built in 1930. The houses have flat roofs, central balconies to the north-facing central bays and alternating entrances. Rendered walls incorporate red-brick panels between front windows and at central bays. Concrete entrance canopies, some early timber windows and front boundary walls with metal gates survive; several houses have been altered.
access_status: Designed by Joseph Downes of McDonnell & Dixon for the Dublin Commercial Public Utility Society. NIAH identifies the group as a good example of the International Style in Irish housing and notes the contribution of its balconies, chimneystacks, canopies and asymmetrical paired-house arrangement to the suburban character of the street.

name: 25 The Stiles Road — International Modern house
historical_significance: Detached irregular-plan multiple-bay single-, two- and three-storey house, built 1935–37. The house has rounded corners, a flat-roofed open-sided porch, flat roofs concealed behind rendered parapets, smooth rendered walls and a mixture of square-headed and rounded-corner windows, including vertical strip windows. A double-leaf steel gate fronts a roughcast rendered boundary wall.
access_status: Designed by Vincent O’Hanlon, this is the only house on The Stiles Road built in a contemporary style, according to the NIAH appraisal. Its curved corners, stepped façade, raised parapets and flat roofs contain subdued Art Deco references and make it an interesting suburban example of the International Modern style.
photography_restrictions: Private residence. Photograph only from the public footpath; do not enter the garden or property. Respect residents' privacy.

name: Clontarf Hospital — historic Blackheath house
historical_significance: Formerly a detached complex-plan multiple-bay three-storey house with dormer attic, built in 1872 and extended in 1879. The historic house has canted bays to the south garden elevation, box bays to the west, and a gabled breakfront and porch to the north entrance elevation. It retains slate roofs, carved timber details, stone and render surrounds, sash windows and interior decorative plasterwork, timber panelling, joinery and stained glass. It is now used as a hospital administration building.
access_status: Designed by Thomas Drew for Gibson Black, a wine merchant and Commissioner of the Township of Clontarf. The descendants of Gibson Black bequeathed the house to the Church of Ireland in 1942, after which the Orthopaedic Hospital occupied it. The building retains much of its Victorian domestic character despite its institutional use.
